title: Twelve months of headlines
body:
## The Rescue, Priced In and Partially Reversed

The twelve months between April 2025 and May 2026 compressed what ordinarily takes a decade of restructuring into a single trading year — and the market's verdict, a rally from a ¥145 low to an intraday high of ¥4,380 followed by a retracement to ¥1,574 at the close of the frozen window, tells a story of euphoria outrunning execution.

The sequence began on **April 30, 2025**, when Unitika executed a capital restructuring that effectively transferred control to the state. The company cancelled all existing Class A and Class B preferred shares and issued Class C preferred shares to the Regional Economy Vitalization Corporation of Japan (REVIC) via a ¥20 billion third-party allotment. REVIC's stake carried 66.76% of voting rights. Simultaneously, the three main lenders — MUFG, Mizuho, and Sumitomo Mitsui Trust — approved debt forgiveness of up to ¥43 billion. The message was unambiguous: without that combined ¥63 billion of support, Unitika could not have serviced its obligations while shedding three quarters of its revenue base.

The stock jumped from the ¥165–175 range it had occupied through early 2025, breaching ¥218 in the days that followed. But the market was pricing a story that hadn't yet happened, and a sell-the-news correction dragged the shares back toward the ¥145 trough — the 52-week floor — through mid-summer, as investors waited for management to demonstrate that the REVIC-backed plan was more than a creditor bailout.

## Fujii Takes the Podium

Two weeks after the capital restructuring, on **May 14, 2025**, Unitika filed its [FY3/25 full-year results](https://www.unitika.co.jp/e/news/news250514.html). The headline revenue of ¥126.4 billion (+6.8%) overstated health; the real signal was in operating profit, which swung from a ¥2.5 billion loss to ¥5.9 billion positive — the first meaningful operating surplus in several years. The net loss of ¥24.3 billion, driven by ¥37.9 billion of asset impairments as the fiber and textile segments were written down to their liquidation values, was widely anticipated and absorbed without panic.

New CEO Fujii Minoru used the May 27 earnings call to articulate three levers: price revision pass-throughs in the industrial segment, structural cost reduction in manufacturing, and the clean severance from Southeast Asian operations. That last point mattered operationally and symbolically — the 2014 pivot to Thailand had consumed capital for a decade with negligible returns, and abandoning it freed both management attention and cash.

## Executing Through the Summer

**August 2025** was a self-imposed deadline: Unitika had committed to reaching binding terms on all divestiture and production-transfer deals in the restructuring segments by then. The quarterly results ([Q1 FY3/26, filed August 6](https://www.unitika.co.jp/e/news/news250806.html)) gave partial confirmation that the operating turnaround was real, though the exact figures were not disclosed in the prepared data. What the market watched was deal closure, not quarterly increments.

**October 2025** delivered the first proof: a buyer was secured for the nonwovens business, as reported by Nonwovens Industry magazine. Nonwovens had been a structurally challenged division — competitive Chinese capacity had compressed margins for years — and the divestiture removed a drag without the kind of protracted auction that often signals desperation.

## The Corporate Split and a New Partnership

**November 4, 2025** brought a [formal company split agreement](https://www.unitika.co.jp/e/news/news251104.html) with a wholly owned subsidiary, the legal mechanism for ring-fencing the divested businesses and transferring their liabilities cleanly. The H1 financial results, published a week later on [November 11](https://www.unitika.co.jp/e/news/news251111.html), were the operational backdrop against which the split was announced.

December produced the most strategically interesting disclosure of the period: a joint PPS (polyphenylene sulfide) film development with DIC Corporation, targeting millimeter-wave radar and next-generation communications PCB substrates — previewed under the CES 2026 banner. PPS film for mmWave sits at the intersection of two durable demand curves: 5G/6G infrastructure buildout and automotive radar proliferation. Unitika contributed its polymer processing expertise; DIC brought resin chemistry and distribution reach. The partnership flagged that the residual Unitika — the entity post-restructuring — had genuine technology to sell, not merely assets to wind down.

## The Number That Re-rated the Stock

The decisive data point arrived on **February 5–6, 2026**: [third-quarter FY3/26 consolidated results](https://www.unitika.co.jp/e/news/news260206.html) showing nine-month cumulative revenue of ¥95.6 billion (+2.2%) and, more importantly, operating profit of ¥9.0 billion — up **110.3%** on the prior-year nine months. The equity ratio stood at 25.2%, a figure that, while still modest by Japanese industrial standards, represented a materially healthier balance sheet than the negative equity territory of eighteen months prior.

The market's reaction was extreme. Shares that had languished in the ¥150–¥200 band through most of the second half of 2025 broke out decisively: the trajectory ran from ¥247 to ¥369, then ¥564, ¥922, ¥1,072, ¥1,372, ¥1,792, ¥2,192 — each leg accompanied by volume spikes that in the peak week exceeded 50 million shares daily, against a pre-restructuring norm of roughly 300,000–500,000. The stock hit an intraday high of **¥4,380** sometime in the March–April 2026 window, implying a market capitalisation that the underlying earnings — ¥9.0 billion in nine months annualises to roughly ¥12 billion — struggled to justify at any conventional multiple.

An [April 6, 2026 press release](https://www.unitika.co.jp/news/io-pdf/re20260406-02.pdf) appears to have been a secondary catalyst, though the PDF binary was not parsed in the research pipeline and its precise content remains unverified here.

## What the ¥1,574 Close Implies

By May 22, 2026, the stock had retraced to ¥1,574 — still roughly ten times the ¥145 trough, but 64% off the peak. The correction reflects a familiar dynamic in distressed-turnaround trades: the first profitable quarters get priced at growth-stock multiples, and when the growth rate inevitably moderates — or when the next catalyst (full-year results, Tusco Thailand divestiture, a semiconductor glass-fiber design win announcement) fails to materialise on schedule — the multiple compresses sharply.

Three forward catalysts will determine whether ¥1,574 represents base or dead-cat-bounce: closure of the Tusco Thailand manufacturing transfer (which would complete the geographic retreat and free remaining cash), incremental glass-fiber design wins in semiconductor packaging applications (where the per-substrate economics are orders of magnitude better than apparel-grade fiber), and the FY3/26 full-year results due May 2026. The last item lands inside the frozen window and may already be public — but its contents, and whether operating momentum held through Q4, remain the unresolved question hanging over every valuation exercise in this dossier.
